parts.problemMd:
Potassium permanganate is a purple solid that is soluble in water. A crystal of potassium permanganate is placed in a beaker containing water

After a short time, the crystal becomes smaller and the liquid at the bottom of the beaker becomes purple. Which statement explains this observation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — the crystal dissolves in the water.**

The purple colour spreads because the potassium permanganate crystal dissolves in the water at the bottom of the beaker, putting coloured particles into solution that then move around. The other options describe changes that are not happening here: condensation (A) is a gas turning into a liquid, evaporation (C) is a liquid turning into a gas, and freezing (D) is a liquid turning into a solid — none of these explains a crystal getting smaller in water.

markPoints.textMd: Answer B: the crystal dissolves in the water

parts.problemMd: Which statement describes the final appearance of the liquid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — all of the liquid is purple.**

Given enough time, the dissolved particles diffuse throughout the whole beaker, so the final appearance is a uniformly purple solution. B is wrong because the crystal has completely dissolved, so it cannot remain as a solid; C is wrong because the particles have spread out (diffused) rather than staying near the bottom; and D is wrong because only the top half being purple would mean the spreading was still unfinished — diffusion does not stop halfway up the beaker.

parts.problemMd: Which process causes this change in appearance?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: C — diffusion.**

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, which is exactly how the dissolved permanganate particles spread from the bottom of the beaker until the liquid is evenly purple. Condensation (A) and crystallisation (B) are changes of state, not spreading of particles, and sublimation (D) is a solid turning directly into a gas.

markPoints.textMd: Answer C: diffusion

parts.problemMd: The formula of potassium permanganate is KMnO4 How many different elements are there in potassium permanganate?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — 3 different elements.**

KMnO₄ contains potassium (K), manganese (Mn) and oxygen (O) — three different elements. B (4) counts the four oxygen atoms as if they were four elements, but they are all one element; C (6) and D (7) do not correspond to any count in the formula — there are neither six nor seven different kinds of atom present, only three.

markPoints.textMd: Answer A: 3

parts.problemMd: Elements L and M are in the same group. State why they have similar chemical reactions.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.**

Elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell (the same number of valence electrons). It is these outer electrons that take part in chemical reactions, so atoms with the same outer-shell arrangement react in similar ways.

parts.problemMd: An atom of element Q has 31 protons. Use this information to explain how you can determine the number of protons in an atom of element R.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: R has 33 protons — two more than Q.**

Q and R are in the same period, with R immediately after Q. Moving one place to the right across a period adds exactly one proton to the nucleus (the atomic number increases by 1). So R's atomic number is 31 + 2 = 33, because the atomic number of R is two more (than Q). The number of protons identifies the element, and R's is determined by its position, not by its electrons or mass number.

parts.problemMd:
A student does these two tests on a solution made from a white solid.

| Test | Result |
| --- | --- |
| flame test | red flame |
| add acidified silver nitrate solution | cream precipitate |

Give the formula of the ion that produces the red flame.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Li⁺ (a lithium ion).**

A crimson-red flame is the characteristic flame test colour for lithium ions. (Sr²⁺ also gives a red flame, so it is accepted as well.) The flame colour arises because the ion's electrons are excited and emit light of a characteristic colour as they fall back.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: silver bromide, AgBr.**

A cream precipitate with silver nitrate is the positive test for bromide ions: Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s). The cream colour distinguishes it from silver chloride (white) and silver iodide (yellow).

parts.problemMd: State why the wire should be clean when used in the flame test.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: impurities (other ions) could alter the flame colour and interfere with the results.**

If the wire carries leftover ions from a previous sample or from dirt, those ions give their own flame colours. The colour you see would then be a mixture, so you could not tell which metal ion you are testing — the results of the test would be unreliable.

A student uses this apparatus to investigate the colours in four different inks, A, B, C and D

Explain two mistakes the student made when setting up his experiment. 1 2
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the two mistakes are (1) the baseline was drawn in ink, and (2) the water level was above the ink spots.**

*Mistake 1:* the baseline has been drawn in **ink** rather than pencil. Ink is a mixture of dyes that dissolves in the solvent and moves up the paper, so it will interfere with the results — the dye spots mix with the baseline and contaminate them. Pencil is insoluble, so a pencil baseline stays put.

*Mistake 2:* the water level is **above** the ink spots (baseline). The dyes would simply dissolve into the water at the bottom instead of travelling up the paper, so the inks mix with the water rather than separating — no chromatogram results.

parts.problemMd:
In 1937 an airship full of hydrogen gas flew from Germany to America.

Which property of hydrogen makes it a suitable gas to use in an airship?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: C — it has a low density.**

An airship floats because the gas inside is less dense than air, giving lift. Colour (A) and solubility (B) are irrelevant, and hydrogen does not conduct electricity (D). The key usable property of hydrogen for an airship is its very low density.

markPoints.textMd: Answer C: low density

parts.problemMd: Explain why helium is now used in airships instead of hydrogen.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: helium is inert (unreactive), hydrogen is flammable/explosive.**

*M1:* helium is a noble gas — it is inert and does not react with the air/oxygen around the airship, so it cannot catch fire (it is not flammable or explosive).

*M2:* hydrogen, by contrast, is flammable — it reacts explosively with oxygen in the air. That is why hydrogen airships were abandoned for helium, even though both gases are less dense than air.

parts.problemMd: State why a catalyst is used in this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: to increase the rate of reaction (speed the reaction up).**

The catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed per second and the ammonia is made faster. Note the marks are for the rate — a catalyst never changes the position of equilibrium or the yield; it only makes equilibrium be reached more quickly.

parts.problemMd:
The reactions of metals with water and with dilute sulfuric acid can be used to determine the order of reactivity of the metals. The table shows the reactions of four metals, W, X, Y and Z, with water and with dilute sulfuric acid

![metals reactivity table — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.11)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2019-06/4CH1-1C/assets/asset_6_stem_reactivity-table.png)

What is the order of reactivity of these metals? most reactive least reactive
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B (most reactive → least reactive: Z, X, Y, W).**

Reading the table: Z reacts violently with acid and quickly with water — the most vigorous reactions — so Z is most reactive. X reacts slowly with water but quickly with acid, Y reacts with acid but not water, and W shows no reaction with either. That puts the order Z > X > Y > W, which is option B. A puts W first, which cannot be right because W is the least reactive; C and D both place Z (or X) in the wrong position because they miss that water is the harder reaction to achieve — reactivity is judged by how vigorously the metals react with *both* reagents.

parts.problemMd: State which metal, W, X, Y or Z, could be copper.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: W.**

Copper does not react with dilute sulfuric acid or with water — in the table, W is the only metal with no reaction in either. So W could be copper (a metal below hydrogen in the reactivity series).

**Answer: X.**

parts.problemMd: A displacement reaction can also be used to decide the order of reactivity of two metals. State two observations made when an excess of magnesium powder is added to an aqueous solution of copper(II) sulfate. 1 2
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: a brown solid forms and the solution turns colourless.**

Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate: Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu.

*Observation 1:* a brown/pink-brown solid forms — this is the copper metal displaced from the solution (a precipitate).

*Observation 2:* the blue solution turns colourless — the blue Cu²⁺ ions are removed from solution as copper metal, leaving colourless magnesium sulfate.

Explain why silicon dioxide has a high melting point.

parts.problemMd: Explain why graphite conducts electricity.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: graphite has delocalised electrons that can flow.**

*M1:* each carbon atom in graphite is bonded to only three others, so one outer electron per atom is delocalised — free to move along the layers (a "sea" of delocalised electrons).

*M2:* these charged, mobile electrons can flow through the structure when a voltage is applied, carrying the current — that is why graphite conducts electricity (unlike diamond, where all four outer electrons are locked in bonds).

parts.problemMd: State why diamond is hard but graphite is soft.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond has a rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice; graphite's layers can slide.**

*Diamond is hard:* every carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a giant 3D tetrahedral lattice — a rigid network of strong bonds in all directions that resists scratching.

*Graphite is soft:* each atom bonds to only three others, forming layers. The layers are held together by weak forces, so they can slide over each other easily (which is why graphite marks paper).

parts.problemMd:
Ethene (C2H4) can be converted into chloroethene (C2H3Cl) in a two-stage process.

The first stage is to convert ethene into 1,2-dichloroethane, C2H4Cl2 Ethene is reacted with hydrogen chloride and oxygen. Complete the chemical equation for this reaction C2H4 + HCl + O2 → C2H4Cl2 + H2O
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2C₂H₄ + 4HCl + O₂ → 2C₂H₄Cl₂ + 2H₂O (multiples and fractions accepted).**

Balance one element at a time on the skeleton C₂H₄ + HCl + O₂ → C₂H₄Cl₂ + H₂O:

- *Chlorine:* C₂H₄Cl₂ carries 2 Cl, so HCl needs a 2.
- *Hydrogen:* left = 4 (from C₂H₄) + 2 (from 2HCl) = 6; right = 4 (in C₂H₄Cl₂) + 2c, so c = 1 H₂O.
- *Oxygen:* 1 O on the right needs half an O₂, so ½ O₂.

That gives C₂H₄ + 2HCl + ½O₂ → C₂H₄Cl₂ + H₂O; doubling every coefficient clears the fraction: **2C₂H₄ + 4HCl + O₂ → 2C₂H₄Cl₂ + 2H₂O**.

parts.problemMd: In the second stage, 1,2-dichloroethane is converted into chloroethene. C2H4Cl2 → C2H3Cl + HCl This is a thermal decomposition reaction. State what is meant by the term thermal decomposition.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: breaking down (decomposing) by heating.**

"Thermal" tells you the energy source is heat and "decomposition" tells you one substance breaks into simpler ones. So thermal decomposition is breaking a compound down into simpler substances by heating it — here C₂H₄Cl₂ splits into C₂H₃Cl and HCl when heated.

parts.problemMd: The boiling point of Halon 1301 is −58 °C. Explain why Halon 1301 has a low boiling point.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: its intermolecular forces are weak, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.**

parts.problemMd:
The gas burned in a Bunsen burner is methane. The equation for the complete combustion of methane is CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g)

Calculate the mass of oxygen required to react with 32 g of methane. [Mr of methane = 16] mass of oxygen = g
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 128 g of oxygen.**

*Step 1 — moles of methane:* n(CH₄) = 32 ÷ 16 = 2 mol.

*Step 2 — moles of oxygen:* from CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, each mole of methane needs 2 moles of oxygen, so n(O₂) = 2 × 2 = 4 mol.

*Step 3 — mass of oxygen:* mass = moles × Mr = 4 × 32 = 128 g.

Explain why water collects in the U-tube.

![apparatus: methane flame, U-tube in ice and water, limewater flask, to pump — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.16)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2019-06/4CH1-1C/assets/asset_11_stem_apparatus.png)

parts.problemMd: Show that the heat energy change, Q, is about 2400 J. [mass of 1.00 cm3 of solution = 1.00 g] [for the solution, c = 4.18 J/g/ °C ] Q = J
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Q ≈ 2400 J (calculation gives −2420 J).**

*Step 1 — temperature change:* ΔT = 14.2 − 20.0 = −5.8 °C.

*Step 2 — substitute into Q = mcΔT:* the solution's mass is 100 cm³ × 1.00 g/cm³ = 100 g, so
Q = 100 × 4.18 × (−5.8) = −2420 J.

*Step 3:* −2420 J is "about 2400 J", as the question asks. The negative sign shows the energy came *out of* the surroundings — consistent with the endothermic dissolution.

parts.problemMd: Use your answer to part (b) to calculate the enthalpy change, ∆H, in kilojoules per mole of ammonium nitrate. [Mr of ammonium nitrate = 80.0] Include a sign in your answer. ∆H = kJ/mol

*Step 1 — moles of ammonium nitrate:* n = 8.00 ÷ 80.0 = 0.100 mol.

*Step 2 — energy per mole:* 2420 J ÷ 0.100 mol = 24200 J/mol = 24.2 kJ/mol (any number of significant figures accepted).

*Step 3 — sign:* the mixture cooled, so the dissolving is endothermic and ΔH is **positive: ΔH = +24.2 kJ/mol**. (A correct answer with no working and no/incorrect sign scores 3 of the 4 marks.)

parts.problemMd: Explain why the chemical formula of ammonium sulfate is (NH4)2SO4 Refer to the charges on the ions in your answer.

**Answer: because the charges must cancel — two 1+ ammonium ions balance one 2− sulfate ion.**
The ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, carries a single positive charge, while the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, carries two negative charges. parts.problemMd: Describe how compound D can be obtained from crude oil using the industrial process of fractional distillation.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: heat the crude oil until it vaporises, pass the vapour into a fractionating column, let the fractions separate by boiling point, and collect compound D at the top of the column in the refinery gas fraction.**
*Step 1.* The crude oil is heated in a furnace so that it boils and vaporises.
*Step 2.* The hot vapour passes into the fractionating column (tower), which is hottest at the bottom and cooler towards the top — a temperature gradient.
*Step 3.* The column separates the mixture: each hydrocarbon condenses (or stays as a gas) at the height where the temperature matches its own boiling point, so the compounds in crude oil separate because of their different boiling points.
*Step 4.* Compound D is propane (C₃H₈), whose molecules are small with very low boiling points, so it rises to the top without condensing and is collected there, in the refinery gas fraction.

*Step 2:* Divide both results by the smallest value to obtain the simplest ratio:
For lead: 0.42 ÷ 0.42 = 1
For oxygen: 0.84 ÷ 0.42 = 2

This gives a ratio of 1:2 for lead to oxygen, which corresponds to the formula PbO₂, lead(IV) oxide.

parts.problemMd: A student is given a sample of solid red lead oxide and some dilute nitric acid. Describe how the student could obtain a pure dry sample of lead(II) nitrate crystals.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: warm the dilute nitric acid, add the red lead oxide and stir, filter off the insoluble solids, then crystallise the lead(II) nitrate from the filtrate by heating, cooling and filtering again, and dry the crystals gently.**
*Step 1 — react.* Warm the dilute nitric acid in a beaker (gently — it must not be boiled) and add the red lead oxide a little at a time, stirring so the acid reaches all of the solid. The reaction forms lead(II) nitrate, which dissolves, while the insoluble lead(IV) oxide and any unreacted red lead oxide stay solid.
*Step 2 — filter.* Filter the mixture. The filtrate is the lead(II) nitrate solution; the residue on the filter paper is the unwanted insoluble material.
*Step 3 — concentrate.* Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to boil off some of the water. Every so often dip a glass rod in and let a drop cool on it: when small crystals form on the glass rod, stop heating.
*Step 4 — crystallise.* Leave the concentrated solution to cool so more lead(II) nitrate crystals form as the solution becomes saturated, then filter the crystals off.
*Step 5 — dry.* Dry the crystals by pressing them between filter papers or leaving them somewhere warm — never over a hot Bunsen flame, which would spit the crystals away or scorch them. That leaves a pure, dry sample of lead(II) nitrate crystals.

**Answer: the empirical formula is C₂H₅.**

parts.problemMd: Deduce the molecular formula of this alkane.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: C4H10**

The molecular formula of an alkane follows the general formula CnH2n+2. Using the empirical formula C2H5:

*Step 1:* The empirical formula has 2 carbon atoms and 5 hydrogen atoms.
*Step 2:* For alkanes, the general formula is CnH2n+2. For n=2: C2H(2×2)+2 = C2H6
*Step 3:* Since C2H5 is not in the form CnH2n+2, we need to find a multiple that works.
*Step 4:* If we double the empirical formula (C2H5) × 2 = C4H10
*Step 5:* Check if C4H10 fits the alkane formula: CnH2n+2 = C4H(2×4)+2 = C4H10

Therefore, the molecular formula is C4H10 (butane).

parts.problemMd: The equation for the complete combustion of one mole of an alkane can be represented by alkane + ZO2 → XCO2 + YH2O Complete combustion of one mole of the alkane produces 308 g of carbon dioxide and 144 g of water. X, Y and Z are the numbers used to balance the equation. Calculate the values of X, Y and Z. [Mr of CO2 = 44, Mr of H2O = 18] X = Y = Z =
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: X = 7, Y = 8, Z = 11**

*Step 1:* Calculate the moles of carbon dioxide produced:
- Moles of CO2 = mass ÷ Mr = 308g ÷ 44g/mol = 7 mol
- Since each CO2 molecule contains 1 carbon atom, X = 7

*Step 2:* Calculate the moles of water produced:
- Moles of H2O = mass ÷ Mr = 144g ÷ 18g/mol = 8 mol
- Since each H2O molecule contains 2 hydrogen atoms, the alkane must have produced 16 hydrogen atoms
- Therefore, Y = 8

*Step 3:* Determine the molecular formula of the alkane:
- From CO2, we know the alkane contains 7 carbon atoms
- From H2O, we know the alkane contains 16 hydrogen atoms
- So the alkane is C7H16

*Step 4:* Balance the equation C7H16 + ZO2 → 7CO2 + 8H2O
- Carbon is balanced (7 on each side)
- Hydrogen is balanced (16 on each side)
- For oxygen: on the right side we have (7×2) + (8×1) = 14 + 8 = 22 oxygen atoms
- Therefore, Z = 11 (since 11 O2 molecules provide 22 oxygen atoms)

The balanced equation is: C7H16 + 11O2 → 7CO2 + 8H2O

parts.problemMd: Explain, using particle collision theory, how increasing the temperature affects the rate of a reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** Increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction because particles gain kinetic energy, move faster, collide more frequently, and more collisions have energy greater than the activation energy.

*Step 1:* When the temperature of a reaction mixture increases, the rate of reaction increases because the particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.

*Step 2:* With particles moving faster, there are more collisions per unit time between reactant particles.

*Step 3:* More importantly, a greater proportion of these collisions have energy greater than the activation energy required for the reaction to occur.

*Step 4:* As a result, more collisions are successful, meaning more reactant particles are converted into products per unit time, which increases the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd: Determine the empirical formula of the lead oxide. empirical formula of the lead oxide

**Answer:** Pb₃O₄

*Step 1:* Calculate the moles of lead and oxygen using their atomic masses (Pb = 207, O = 16).
Moles of lead = mass ÷ atomic mass = 4.66 g ÷ 207 g/mol = 0.0225 mol

*Step 3:* Multiply by 3 to get whole numbers (since 1.33 is approximately 4/3).
Lead: 1 × 3 = 3
Oxygen: 1.33 × 3 = 4

*Step 4:* The empirical formula is Pb₃O₄.

**Answer: zinc is more reactive than iron, so it reacts in preference to the iron.**

Zinc sits higher than iron in the reactivity series. parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy.**

*Step 1:* A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway or route for the reaction to occur.

parts.problemMd: Explain how increasing the pressure of gases increases the rate of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Increasing pressure brings particles closer together, leading to more frequent collisions per unit time.**

*Step 1:* When the pressure of gases is increased, the particles or molecules are forced closer together. This means there are more particles in a given volume or space.
*Step 2:* With the particles closer together, there are more collisions occurring between them.
*Step 3:* These collisions happen more frequently per unit time, which increases the rate of reaction.

This question is about barium chloride.

Barium chloride can be made by reacting barium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid. The chemical equation for the reaction is BaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → BaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g) Describe a method to produce dry crystals of hydrated barium chloride, starting with barium carbonate powder and dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: react the dilute hydrochloric acid with excess barium carbonate, filter, crystallise the filtrate, then dry the crystals gently.**

- Add the barium carbonate powder to the dilute hydrochloric acid in a beaker, one spatula-measure at a time, stirring between additions; the mixture fizzes as carbon dioxide is released.
- Keep adding until the fizzing stops and some solid barium carbonate is left on the bottom: the carbonate is now in excess, so every trace of acid has reacted and the crystals will not be contaminated with acid.
- Filter to remove the excess solid; the filtrate is a solution of barium chloride.
- Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the water, stopping when crystals begin to form on a glass rod dipped into the solution — do not boil all the water away at this stage.
- Leave the hot, concentrated solution to cool slowly so that crystals of hydrated barium chloride form.
- Filter the crystals from the remaining solution, then leave them to dry in a warm place (on filter paper, in a warm oven or in a desiccator) to give dry hydrated crystals.

Evaporating only until crystallisation starts, then drying gently, keeps the water of crystallisation inside the crystals so they stay hydrated.

**Answer:** Graphite has a giant covalent structure with strong covalent bonds throughout, requiring a lot of energy to break. C60 fullerene has a simple molecular structure with weaker intermolecular forces between molecules.

Graphite is a giant covalent structure where each carbon atom is bonded to three others in layers. To melt graphite, these strong covalent bonds must be broken, which requires a lot of energy. **Answer: 5.6 cm³**

*Step 2:* Calculate the moles of hydrated zinc sulfate:

Volume of H₂O = 5.63 g ÷ 1.00 g/cm³ = 5.6 cm³ (to 1 decimal place)

parts.problemMd: Ethane (C2H6) and ethene (C2H4) both react with bromine. Describe the differences in the reactions of ethane and ethene with bromine. Refer to the conditions, the products and the types of reaction involved.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane reacts with bromine only in ultraviolet light, by substitution, making bromoethane and hydrogen bromide; ethene reacts readily without UV, by addition across its double bond, making dibromoethane.**

Ethane, C₂H₆, is saturated, so a C–H bond must break for anything to happen: ethane needs UV radiation as its condition, and a bromine atom swaps in for a hydrogen — C₂H₆ + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + HBr. Swapping an atom in for another is substitution.

Ethene, C₂H₄, is unsaturated: its C=C bond opens and each carbon picks up a bromine atom — C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. Adding atoms across a double bond is addition, and it needs no UV at all.

That is five differences: the condition (UV for ethane only), the bond broken (a C–H bond in ethane, the C=C bond in ethene), the type of reaction (substitution versus addition) and the products (bromoethane + HBr versus dibromoethane) — any five of the following earn the full credit.

parts.problemMd:
Diamond and graphite are made of carbon atoms, joined together by covalent bonds. The diagram shows their structures.

![diagram — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.21)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2022-06/4CH1-1C/assets/asset_8_b_diagram.png)

Discuss the differences between diamond and graphite. Refer to structure and bonding, electrical conductivity and hardness in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond is hard and does not conduct electricity, while graphite is soft and conducts electricity — the differences come from how the carbon atoms are bonded and arranged.**

Structure and bonding: in diamond each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a giant tetrahedral structure. In graphite each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms, forming hexagonal rings arranged in flat layers.

Electrical conductivity: diamond does not conduct electricity because all of its outer electrons are locked in covalent bonds — there are no delocalised electrons to move and carry charge. Graphite conducts electricity because each carbon atom has one electron not used in bonding; these delocalised electrons move along the layers when a voltage is applied.

Hardness: diamond is very hard — to scratch or cut it, many strong C–C covalent bonds need to be broken. Graphite is soft and slippery because the weak forces between its layers let the layers slide over each other, which is why graphite works as a lubricant and in pencils.

parts.problemMd:
Fertilisers add nitrogen to the soil to help plants grow. Ammonia and ammonium sulfate can both be used as fertilisers. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using each of these compounds as fertilisers. Use information from the table in your answer. [pH of rainwater is approximately 5.6]

parts.solutionMd: **Answer:** Ammonia has a higher percentage of nitrogen (82%) compared to ammonium sulfate (21%), making it more efficient at adding nitrogen to the soil. However, ammonia is a gas that is difficult to handle directly and must be dissolved in water before application, which can lead to wastage. Additionally, ammonia has a high pH of 11, which will make the soil alkaline and may damage plants or stunt their growth. Ammonium sulfate, with a pH of 5.5, is closer to the pH of rainwater (approximately 5.6) and will not significantly alter the soil pH, making it safer for plants. However, ammonium sulfate has a lower percentage of nitrogen, so larger amounts are needed to provide the same amount of nitrogen. Both compounds are soluble, which can lead to runoff, wastage of fertiliser, water pollution, and eutrophication if not properly managed.

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: These are two methods used to dispose of the polymer. • burying in landfill sites • burning Discuss the environmental problems caused by these two methods of disposal.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:**

Burying polymers in landfill sites causes environmental problems because polymers are inert and do not biodegrade, meaning they remain in the environment indefinitely. parts.problemMd:
The box gives some methods that are involved in the separation of mixtures. chromatography crystallisation dissolving evaporating filtering fractional distillation simple distillation

Give the best method for obtaining gasoline from crude oil.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: fractional distillation.** Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons whose boiling points increase as their molecules get bigger. The oil is heated so most of it vaporises, and the vapours rise up a fractionating column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Each fraction, including gasoline, condenses at the height where the column temperature matches its boiling range, so the mixture is separated.

parts.problemMd: Give the best method for separating the dyes in black ink.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: chromatography.** A spot of black ink is put near the bottom of some absorbent paper and the paper is dipped in solvent. Each dye in the ink dissolves to a different extent and is attracted differently to the paper, so the dyes travel up the paper at different speeds and separate into distinct spots. This is exactly what chromatography is designed to do — separate the substances in a mixture so they can be identified.

markPoints.textMd: chromatography

parts.problemMd: Give the best method for obtaining pure water from seawater.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: simple distillation.** The seawater is heated in a flask until pure water boils off and evaporates. The vapour travels into a water-cooled condenser, where it turns back into liquid and is collected — that distillate is pure water, because the dissolved salt has a very high boiling point and stays behind in the flask. Distillation is the best choice whenever you need to obtain the solvent itself from a solution.

parts.solutionMd: **Answer: first dissolving, then filtering, then evaporating, then crystallisation.** Copper(II) sulfate is soluble while copper(II) oxide is insoluble, and that difference is what the separation exploits. Finally let the hot, concentrated solution cool slowly so that crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate form — crystallisation gives a pure solid sample.

parts.problemMd: A student mixes the following pairs of solutions. Pair 1 bromine solution and potassium chloride solution Pair 2 bromine solution and potassium iodide solution Explain how the student can use the results of these experiments to show the order of reactivity of the three halogens, bromine, chlorine and iodine. **Answer: Pair 1 shows chlorine is more reactive than bromine, and Pair 2 shows bromine is more reactive than iodine — so the overall order of reactivity is chlorine > bromine > iodine.**

Pair 1: bromine solution mixed with potassium chloride solution. Nothing happens — there is no reaction and no change in colour; the mixture stays yellow/orange. A halogen can only displace the halogen beneath it in the reactivity order, and here the bromine does not react with the chloride ions to produce chlorine — which can only be because bromine is the less reactive of the two. So chlorine is more reactive than bromine.

Pair 2: bromine solution mixed with potassium iodide solution. This time the mixture turns brown (an orange-brown tinge counts too): the bromine has displaced iodine from its iodide ions, and the brown colour is the iodine released — Br₂ + 2KI → I₂ + 2KBr. Displacement only works when the halogen added is the more reactive one, so bromine is more reactive than iodine.

Combining the experiments: chlorine > bromine from Pair 1 and bromine > iodine from Pair 2, which fixes the order of reactivity as chlorine > bromine > iodine.

parts.problemMd: Catalysts can be used to speed up reactions. Describe how a catalyst works.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: a catalyst works by providing an alternative pathway (route) for the reaction, one with a lower activation energy.** Because the energy barrier is lower, a greater proportion of the colliding particles have enough energy to react when they meet, so the number of successful collisions per second rises — that is why catalysts speed reactions up, increasing the rate. parts.problemMd: Explain why straight‑chain alkenes always have the same empirical formula, but straight‑chain alkanes have different empirical formulae. Refer to the molecular formulae of the alkanes C2H6 and C4H10 in your answer.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: Every straight-chain alkene reduces to the same empirical formula, CH₂, but straight-chain alkanes give different empirical formulae because their hydrogen-to-carbon ratio changes with chain length.** In any alkene the number of hydrogen atoms is exactly twice the number of carbon atoms — the general formula is CnH2n — so dividing by the number of carbons always leaves CH₂; ethene (C₂H₄) and propene (C₃H₆) both reduce to CH₂. parts.problemMd: Describe how a pure, dry sample of hydrated zinc nitrate crystals could be obtained from the filtrate.

**Answer: heat the filtrate to evaporate some of the water so a saturated solution forms, leave it to cool so crystals form, filter the crystals off, then dry them.**

parts.problemMd: One mole of Z contains 6.0 × 10²³ atoms. Calculate the number of electrons in one mole of atoms of element Z. Give your answer in standard form. number of electrons =
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 7.2 × 10²⁴ electrons.**

*Step 1 — electrons in one atom:* the Z atom has 12 electrons (its shells hold 2, then 12 − 2 − 2 = 8, then 2 — and the nucleus holds 12 protons, so the atom is neutral overall).

*Step 2 — scale up to one mole:* one mole contains 6.0 × 10²³ atoms, so the number of electrons = 12 × 6.0 × 10²³.

parts.problemMd:
Calcium bromide is an ionic compound. The table shows the formulae and melting points of caffeine and calcium bromide. Name Formula Melting point in °C caffeine C8H10N4O2 235 calcium bromide CaBr2 730 The relative formula mass of calcium bromide is similar to the relative formula mass of caffeine. Explain why calcium bromide has a much higher melting point than caffeine.

![table — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.9)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2024-06/4CH1-1C/assets/asset_4_c_table.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: calcium bromide is a giant ionic lattice held together by strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions, while caffeine is simple molecular with only weak intermolecular forces between its molecules — so far more energy is needed to melt calcium bromide (730 °C) than caffeine (235 °C).**

In solid calcium bromide, Ca²⁺ and Br⁻ ions are packed into a giant lattice. Every ion pulls electrostatically on all of its oppositely charged neighbours, and those strong attractions run throughout the whole structure, so a huge amount of energy is needed to separate the ions before the solid can melt.

Caffeine, C₈H₁₀N₄O₂, has a simple molecular structure: the atoms inside each molecule are joined by strong covalent bonds, but between neighbouring molecules there are only weak intermolecular forces. Melting only has to overcome those weak intermolecular forces — the covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken — so much less energy is needed. That is why a similar relative formula mass still leaves the two melting points (730 °C and 235 °C) far apart: it is the structure and bonding that decide the melting point, not the Mr.

parts.problemMd: What is the formula of ammonium carbonate?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — (NH₄)₂CO₃.**

The ammonium ion is NH₄⁺ (charge 1+) and the carbonate ion is CO₃²⁻ (charge 2−), so two NH₄⁺ ions are needed to balance one CO₃²⁻ ion, giving (NH₄)₂CO₃. A, NH₃CO₃, is wrong because NH₃ is ammonia — an uncharged molecule, not the ammonium ion. B, (NH₃)₂CO₃, is wrong for the same reason: it uses ammonia instead of NH₄⁺. C, NH₄CO₃, is wrong because one 1+ charge cannot cancel one 2− charge.

parts.problemMd: A technician finds an unlabelled bottle on a shelf that could be ammonium carbonate solution. Describe tests that the technician should do to confirm that the solution contains ammonium ions and carbonate ions.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ammonium ions — add sodium hydroxide solution and warm (heat) the mixture, then test the gas given off with damp red litmus paper: it turns blue. Carbonate ions — add dilute hydrochloric acid and test the gas given off with limewater: it turns cloudy/milky.**

For the ammonium test: adding sodium hydroxide and warming releases ammonia gas from the ammonium ions (NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O). Hold damp red litmus paper at the gas — ammonia is alkaline, so the paper turns blue. The litmus must test the gas coming off, not be dipped into the solution.

For the carbonate test: acid plus a carbonate gives carbon dioxide gas, so fizzing starts as soon as the hydrochloric acid is added. Bubble the gas into limewater: the CO₂ turns the limewater cloudy/milky because a white precipitate of insoluble calcium carbonate forms. Again, the limewater tests the gas escaping from the solution — it is never poured straight into the sample.

**Answer: D — chlorine has the strongest forces of attraction between its molecules.**

parts.problemMd:
This question is about alkanes and alkenes.

Give a reason why ethane does not undergo an addition reaction with bromine.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane is saturated — it contains single bonds only, with no double bond.**
An addition reaction needs a C=C double bond that can open up and take extra atoms on across it. In ethane (C₂H₆) every carbon–carbon bond is a single covalent bond and each carbon already has its full share of hydrogen atoms, so bromine atoms have nowhere to add without first breaking bonds. That is why ethane reacts with bromine only by substitution under special conditions, while ethene, with its double bond, adds bromine readily.

parts.problemMd: Complete the equation for the substitution reaction between ethane and bromine, including an essential condition for the reaction. C2H6 + Br2 → + condition
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: C₂H₆ + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + HBr, with ultraviolet light (UV radiation) as the essential condition.**
This is a substitution reaction: in ultraviolet radiation, one bromine atom replaces a hydrogen atom of the ethane. The organic product is bromoethane, C₂H₅Br, and the displaced hydrogen leaves combined with the second bromine atom as hydrogen bromide, HBr. The equation balances (6 H and 2 Br on each side). The condition matters: without UV light the mixture stays unchanged, because an alkane such as ethane simply does not react with bromine in the dark.

parts.problemMd: Give the colour change that occurs when ethene reacts with bromine water.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the bromine water changes from orange to colourless.**
The C=C double bond in ethene opens up and each carbon atom gains a bromine atom, forming colourless 1,2-dibromoethane, so the orange colour of the bromine water is lost — the water is decolourised. parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the structures of lead(II) sulfide and sulfur dioxide. Lead(II) sulfide Sulfur dioxide Explain, in terms of bonding and structure, why lead(II) sulfide is a solid with a very high melting point at room temperature and why sulfur dioxide is a gas at room temperature. lead(II) sulfide sulfur dioxide

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: lead(II) sulfide is a solid with a very high melting point because it is a giant ionic lattice with strong bonds to overcome, while sulfur dioxide is a gas because it is simple molecular with only weak intermolecular forces between its molecules.**

Lead(II) sulfide has a giant ionic structure: a huge lattice of oppositely charged ions, Pb²⁺ and S²⁻. The ionic bonds between these ions are strong electrostatic forces of attraction, and because the ions are held so firmly in place, a lot of energy is needed to break the lattice apart — so a very high temperature is needed to melt it.

Sulfur dioxide is a simple molecular (covalent) substance. Inside each SO₂ molecule the covalent bonds are strong, but the forces between one molecule and the next are weak intermolecular forces. Only a little energy is needed to overcome these weak forces, so the molecules pull apart easily and sulfur dioxide boils far below room temperature, existing as a gas at room temperature.

The wording matters: for lead(II) sulfide talk about ions in a lattice, never molecules; for sulfur dioxide talk about molecules and weak intermolecular forces between them, never ions or ionic bonds.

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: Explain why hexane (C6H14) has a higher boiling point than butane (C4H10).
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: hexane has a higher boiling point because its molecules are larger with longer chains, so there are stronger intermolecular forces between the molecules and more energy is needed to overcome them.**

A C₆H₁₄ molecule is a longer chain than C₄H₁₀, giving more contact between neighbouring molecules, so the intermolecular forces of attraction are stronger in hexane than in butane. Boiling separates the molecules from one another — no covalent bonds are broken — so the stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to overcome them and the higher the temperature at which the liquid boils. Butane has weaker intermolecular forces between its smaller molecules, so they are overcome at a lower temperature and it boils first.

Diamond is a giant covalent structure: every carbon atom is covalently bonded to several others in a rigid 3D network. Because the structure is giant, melting is not a matter of freeing a molecule — strong covalent bonds throughout the whole lattice have to be broken, and there are enormous numbers of them. parts.problemMd: Explain why graphite is soft and is a conductor of electricity. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: graphite is soft because it is layered — strong covalent bonds hold each carbon atom to three others within flat layers, but the weak forces between the layers let them slide over each other — and it conducts electricity because each carbon atom contributes one delocalised electron that is free to move through the solid.**

Structure: in graphite each carbon atom is joined to three other carbon atoms by covalent bonds, so the atoms form flat hexagonal sheets — a 2D layer structure — rather than the 3D network of diamond.

Why it is soft: within a layer the covalent bonds are strong, but the forces between neighbouring layers are weak. Little energy is needed to slide one layer over another, so the layers flake off easily — which is why a pencil leaves graphite on paper and why graphite feels soft.

Why it conducts: because each carbon is bonded to only three neighbours, one outer-shell electron per atom is left out of the bonding. These electrons become delocalised between the layers, and delocalised electrons are free to move through the whole solid. When a voltage is applied they drift along and carry charge, so graphite conducts electricity — unlike diamond, where every outer electron is locked into a covalent bond and nothing can move.

parts.problemMd: Ethane and ethene undergo different types of reaction with bromine. Describe the differences between these two reactions.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane reacts by substitution only in ultraviolet light, decolourising the bromine very slowly (if at all) and making two products — bromoethane and hydrogen bromide; ethene reacts by addition immediately, even in the dark, decolourising the orange bromine straight away and making one product, dibromoethane.**

*Ethane (saturated):* its C−C single bonds are strong, so a substitution reaction happens only when ultraviolet (UV) radiation supplies the energy — one bromine atom replaces a hydrogen atom, producing bromoethane (C₂H₅Br) and hydrogen bromide (HBr). The orange colour of the bromine fades only very slowly, if at all.

*Ethene (unsaturated):* its reactive C=C double bond opens and bromine atoms add across it — an addition reaction that happens immediately, with no light needed. The orange colour turns colourless at once, and the single product is the addition compound dibromoethane (C₂H₄Br₂).

So the differences to state: substitution vs addition, UV light needed vs not needed, decolourising very slowly vs immediately, and two products vs one.

**Answer: argon.**

Argon is a noble gas with a complete outer electron shell, so its atoms are stable on their own and it exists as individual atoms rather than molecules. parts.problemMd:
This question is about atomic structure and the Periodic Table.

Which particle is a proton?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — X is the proton.**

X is drawn inside the nucleus carrying a single positive charge, and a proton is exactly that: the positive particle found in the nucleus. A (W) is the neutron — it also sits in the nucleus but carries no charge, so it cannot be the proton. C (Y) is an electron — a tiny negatively charged particle moving in shells around the nucleus. D (Z) is the nucleus as a whole — the central cluster of protons and neutrons, not one single particle.

markPoints.textMd: Answer B: X

parts.problemMd: Which particle has a relative charge of 0?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — W, the neutron, has a relative charge of 0.**

Neutrons are the neutral particles in the nucleus: they add mass but no charge at all. B (X) cannot be right because X is a proton with a relative charge of +1. C (Y) cannot be right because Y is an electron with a relative charge of −1. D (Z) cannot be right because Z is the nucleus, which contains protons and therefore has an overall positive charge rather than zero.

markPoints.textMd: Answer A: W

parts.problemMd: Name the part of the atom labelled Z.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the nucleus.**

Z points to the compact cluster in the centre of the atom where all the protons and neutrons are gathered; the electrons (labelled Y in the diagram) move around it in shells. Almost the entire mass of the atom is concentrated in this tiny, positively charged nucleus.

markPoints.textMd: Nucleus

parts.problemMd: What is the group number of this element?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — the group number is 3.**

The group number counts the electrons in the outer shell. Counting the electrons drawn in the diagram, this atom has shells holding 2 + 3 = 5 electrons altogether, so three of them sit in the outer shell and the element belongs in group 3. A (2) is wrong because two is the number of occupied shells, which gives the period rather than the group. C (5) is wrong because five is the total number of electrons (the atomic number), not the outer-shell count. D (11) is wrong because an atom with eleven electrons would be a much bigger atom with more shells than the one drawn.

markPoints.textMd: Answer B: 3

parts.problemMd: What is the period number of this element?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — the period number is 2.**

The period number equals the number of occupied shells in the atom, and the diagram shows electrons filling exactly two shells, so this element sits in period 2. B (3) is wrong: three counts the outer-shell electrons, which gives the group. C (5) is wrong: five is the total electron count (the atomic number), not the number of shells. D (11) is wrong: eleven electrons would fill three shells, so it cannot describe this atom.

markPoints.textMd: Answer A: 2

parts.problemMd: Give the chemical symbol of this element.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B.**

Three outer-shell electrons put the element in group 3 and two occupied shells put it in period 2; the atom carries 2 + 3 = 5 electrons, so its atomic number is 5. The element with atomic number 5 is boron — in the table of period 2 elements it falls between Be (atomic number 4) and C (atomic number 6) — and its chemical symbol is B.

markPoints.textMd: B

parts.problemMd: State what type of particle is formed when an atom loses its outer shell electrons.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: a positive ion (a cation).**

Electrons are negatively charged, so when an atom loses its outer-shell electrons it is left with more protons than electrons. The particle that remains has an overall positive charge and is called a positive ion, or cation. It is not an anion — that name is kept for the negatively charged ions formed when atoms gain electrons.

parts.problemMd: Two beakers are unlabelled. One beaker contains a solution of ammonium chloride and the other beaker contains a solution of ammonium sulfate. Describe tests that can be carried out to confirm that one beaker contains ammonium chloride and the other beaker contains ammonium sulfate.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: distinguish the two solutions by testing for the anion, since both contain the same ammonium cation. For the chloride: add a few drops of dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution — a white precipitate confirms chloride ions. For the sulfate: add a few drops of dilute nitric acid (or hydrochloric acid), then add barium chloride solution (barium nitrate works equally well) — a white precipitate confirms sulfate ions.**

The beaker giving the white precipitate with silver nitrate contains the ammonium chloride: the nitric acid is added first to remove carbonate impurities that would otherwise give a false result, and then the silver ions react with chloride ions to form insoluble silver chloride. Do not acidify with hydrochloric acid in this test, because that would add chloride ions of its own and turn white in both beakers.

The beaker giving the white precipitate with barium chloride contains the ammonium sulfate: barium ions react with sulfate ions to form insoluble barium sulfate. Here the acid must not be sulfuric acid, which would add sulfate ions and spoil the test.

So one beaker turns white with silver nitrate (ammonium chloride) and the other turns white with barium chloride after acidifying with nitric or hydrochloric acid (ammonium sulfate).

**Answer: the missing formulae are Mg(NO₃)₂, Li₂SO₄ and AlPO₄.**

The completed set of compounds is therefore: with Li⁺ — LiNO₃, Li₂SO₄ and Li₃PO₄; with Mg²⁺ — Mg(NO₃)₂, MgSO₄ and Mg₃(PO₄)₂; with Al³⁺ — Al(NO₃)₃, Al₂(SO₄)₃ and AlPO₄.

parts.problemMd: Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: both sodium chloride and magnesium oxide are giant ionic lattices held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, but the attractions in MgO are stronger because its ions carry higher charges, so more energy is needed to overcome them — and that is why MgO melts at a higher temperature.**

Both substances are ionic: a giant lattice of positive and negative ions packed in a regular pattern, with every ion pulled from all sides by electrostatic attraction towards the oppositely charged ions around it. These ionic bonds act in every direction and must be overcome for the crystal to melt.

The difference lies in the size of the charges. In MgO the ions are Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, each carrying a double charge, while in NaCl the ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ with only single charges. The ions in MgO therefore have a much higher charge density, so the electrostatic attraction between them is stronger than the attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

Stronger attraction means more energy must be supplied to overcome the forces holding the lattice together, so magnesium oxide has the higher melting point.

parts.problemMd: Which row shows the correct number of products for these reactions? Propene and bromine Propane and bromine
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — one product for propene with bromine and two products for propane with bromine.**

Propene is an alkene: its C=C double bond opens up and both bromine atoms add across it in a single addition reaction, so only one product (a dibromopropane) can form. parts.problemMd: State what is meant by the term functional group.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the functional group is the atom or group of atoms in a molecule that determines its chemical properties — the part of the molecule responsible for its characteristic reactions.**

parts.problemMd:
Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons.

Describe how useful hydrocarbons can be obtained from crude oil. Refer to fractional distillation and cracking in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions, and some of the long-chain fractions are then cracked to make the smaller hydrocarbons that are in high demand.**

*Fractional distillation:* crude oil is heated so most of it evaporates, and the vaporised mixture enters a tall fractionating column with a temperature gradient — it is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. The hydrocarbons in crude oil have different boiling points, so as the vapours rise, each fraction condenses at the temperature where its boiling point is reached: long-chain hydrocarbons with high boiling points condense low down where it is hot, and shorter-chain alkanes with low boiling points keep rising and condense higher up where it is cooler. In this way the mixture is separated into useful fractions.

*Why cracking is needed:* fractional distillation produces far more long-chain hydrocarbons than can be sold, while short-chain alkanes are in much greater demand than the fractions supply — so the excess long-chain fraction is cracked. Cracking is done by heating the hydrocarbon vapours to about 600–700 °C over a catalyst such as silica, alumina or zeolite. It splits large alkane molecules into shorter-chain alkanes, which are more flammable and make better fuels, and into alkenes, which are valuable reactive starting materials used to make polymers (plastics).

**Answer: sulfur impurities in fuels burn to make sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in rain to form acid rain.**

parts.problemMd: Explain why ethane has a lower boiling point than octane.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane has weaker intermolecular forces between its molecules than octane does, so less energy is needed to overcome them.**

Ethane is a small molecule with only two carbon atoms, while octane's long chain of eight carbons gives far more contact between neighbouring molecules and hence stronger intermolecular forces. **Answer: 2,7.**

parts.problemMd: Describe the changes in the electronic configurations of a lithium atom and a fluorine atom when they form lithium fluoride. fluorine lithium
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: fluorine changes from 2.7 to 2.8 — it gains one electron; lithium changes from 2.1 to 2 — it loses one electron.**

Lithium (configuration 2.1) hands its single outer electron over to a fluorine atom. Losing that electron leaves lithium with just the complete first shell, so its arrangement drops from 2.1 to 2 and the atom becomes a Li⁺ ion. Fluorine takes that electron into its outer shell, so its arrangement rises from 2.7 to 2.8, forming a fluoride ion. Both ions finish with full outer shells, which is what drives the transfer.

parts.problemMd: Lithium fluoride has a giant ionic structure. Explain why lithium fluoride has a high melting point.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions takes a lot of heat energy to break, so lithium fluoride has a high melting point.**

LiF is a giant ionic lattice built from Li⁺ and F⁻ ions. parts.problemMd: A student is given an aqueous solution of chlorine and an aqueous solution of potassium bromide. Explain how he can use these two solutions to compare the reactivity of chlorine with the reactivity of bromine.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Mix the aqueous chlorine with the aqueous potassium bromide — the mixture turns orange because bromine is displaced, which proves chlorine is the more reactive of the two halogens.**

Add the chlorine solution to the potassium bromide solution in a test tube. Chlorine sits above bromine in Group 7, and a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one from its salt: the chlorine takes bromine's place in the compound and bromine, Br₂, is set free in the solution. The bromine is what you see — the colourless potassium bromide solution turns orange (any orange/yellow/brown shade counts as the bromine appearing). Ionic equation: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. The observation therefore settles the comparison: because a displacement reaction happens, chlorine is more reactive than bromine. The reverse argument holds too — if no change had been seen, bromine would have been the more reactive of the pair.

**Answer:** Dynamic equilibrium is when the forward and backward reactions occur at the same time at equal rates.

parts.problemMd: Describe how a pure, dry sample of the insoluble salt, barium sulfate, could be made from the two solids sodium sulfate and barium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: dissolve both solids in water, mix the two solutions, filter off the barium sulfate precipitate, wash the residue with distilled water, then dry it between filter papers or in a warm oven.**
*Step 1 — make two solutions.* Sodium sulfate and barium chloride are both soluble, so dissolve each solid in a little distilled water, giving a solution of each of the solids.
*Step 2 — mix.* Pour the two solutions together and stir. Barium sulfate is insoluble, so a white precipitate forms immediately while the sodium chloride stays in solution: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s).
*Step 3 — separate.* Filter the mixture. The residue in the filter paper is the barium sulfate; the sodium chloride solution passes through as the filtrate.
*Step 4 — purify.* Wash the precipitate (the barium sulfate residue) with distilled water to rinse off any sodium chloride solution clinging to it — without washing, dried crystals would carry trapped impurities.
*Step 5 — dry.* Dry the solid between fresh filter papers or leave it in a warm oven. Drying over a hot Bunsen flame is unsuitable: it can scorch the paper and spit fine crystals away, so gentle drying is what gives a pure, dry sample.

A student is given a mixture of salt solution and sand. She wants to obtain pure water from the mixture.

She separates the sand from the salt solution. Which method of separation should she use?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — filtration.**

Sand is an insoluble solid, so filtration separates it from the salt solution: the filter paper holds back the sand grains as the residue while the salt solution passes through as the filtrate. **Answer: Alloys are harder than pure metals because the different sized atoms in an alloy disrupt the regular arrangement of atoms, making it more difficult for layers to slide over each other.**

In a pure metal, all atoms are the same size and arranged in a regular, repeating pattern. This regular arrangement allows layers of atoms to slide over each other easily, which is why pure metals are typically soft and malleable.

In an alloy, atoms of different elements are added to the metal structure. These atoms are often a different size to the original metal atoms. This disrupts the regular arrangement of the lattice structure.

The diagram below illustrates this:

[Diagram showing three layers of atoms. The first and third layers consist of uniform circles representing the pure metal atoms. The middle layer contains circles of two different sizes, with some of the original atoms replaced by smaller atoms representing the alloying element. The different sized atoms disrupt the regular stacking pattern.]

This disruption of the regular arrangement makes it harder for the layers to slide over each other, which is why alloys are harder than pure metals.

parts.problemMd: Explain why this process is carried out in the absence of air and at a temperature below 40 °C.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: air is excluded because oxygen ruins fermentation, and the temperature stays below 40 °C because heat destroys the yeast's enzymes.**

The fermentation reaction needs anaerobic conditions. In air the yeast switches to aerobic respiration: the ethanol that forms reacts with oxygen and is oxidised, so ethanol is not produced — in air it would be oxidised further to ethanoic acid (the acid in vinegar). Aerobic conditions also produce carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol, so keeping air out is what makes the yeast give alcohol.

The temperature matters because fermentation is catalysed by enzymes in the yeast. If the temperature rises above 40 °C the enzymes become denatured — their shape is destroyed — which makes the reaction slow down and finally stop. Yeast works fastest at its optimum temperature, between 30 °C and 40 °C, so the reaction is kept just under 40 °C.

Complete the energy profile diagram for the reaction. Label the enthalpy change for this reaction, ΔH, and the activation energy. Energy 2C4H6 + 11O2

![diagram — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.16)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2020-11/4CH1-2C/assets/asset_5_c_iii_diagram.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** The energy profile diagram should show:
- Reactants (2C4H6 + 11O2) at a higher energy level than products (8CO2 + 6H2O)
- A curve rising from reactants to form an energy maximum (the activated complex) and then falling to the products level
- The activation energy (Ea) shown as the vertical distance between reactants and the energy maximum
- The enthalpy change (ΔH) shown as the vertical distance between reactants and products, with the value -3446 kJ/mol

Since the reaction is exothermic (ΔH is negative), the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants. The activation energy represents the minimum energy required to initiate the reaction.

parts.problemMd: Predict the effect on the yield of CO(g) at equilibrium when the temperature is increased without changing the pressure. Give a reason for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: The yield of CO(g) increases.**

When the temperature is increased, the equilibrium shifts to the right to produce more CO(g). This happens because the forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH = +41 kJ/mol), meaning it absorbs heat. According to Le Chatelier's principle, when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in temperature, the system will shift in the direction that counteracts the change. In this case, increasing the temperature favors the endothermic forward reaction, which produces more CO(g).

parts.problemMd: Predict the effect on the yield of CO(g) at equilibrium when the pressure is increased without changing the temperature. Give a reason for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: There is no effect on the yield of CO(g).**

When the pressure is increased, there is no effect on the yield of CO(g) because there are equal numbers of moles of gas on both sides of the equilibrium equation. The reaction is H₂(g) + CO₂(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂O(g), with 2 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles of gas on the right. According to Le Chatelier's principle, changing the pressure only affects equilibria where there is a different number of moles of gas on each side. Since the number of moles is the same, increasing the pressure does not shift the equilibrium position or change the yield of CO(g).

**Answer: nitrogen.**

Nitrogen makes up around four-fifths of the air — far more than oxygen, which accounts for most of what is left. parts.problemMd: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium. Refer to the electronic configurations of the atoms in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: The electron configuration of sodium is 2,8,1 and potassium is 2,8,8,1. Potassium's outer electron is in the fourth shell, which is further from the nucleus than sodium's outer electron in the third shell. This increased distance means the outer electron in potassium is less attracted to the nucleus and is more easily lost, making potassium more reactive than sodium.**

Sodium has the electron configuration 2,8,1, meaning it has one electron in its outer shell (third shell). Potassium has the electron configuration 2,8,8,1, with its outer electron in the fourth shell. The outer electron in potassium is further from the nucleus than in sodium. As the distance from the nucleus increases, the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron decreases. This weaker attraction means potassium's outer electron is more easily lost during chemical reactions compared to sodium's outer electron, making potassium more reactive.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Fermentation uses renewable sugar cane while hydration uses non-renewable crude oil; fermentation operates at lower temperatures and pressures, reducing energy costs; fermentation uses natural yeast which is not harmful, while hydration uses corrosive phosphoric acid; however, hydration is faster and produces purer ethanol than fermentation.**

The fermentation method has several advantages over hydration. First, it uses sugar cane as a raw material, which is renewable and can be regrown, unlike crude oil which is finite and non-renewable. Second, fermentation operates at much lower temperatures (30°C) and pressures (1 atmosphere) compared to hydration (300°C and 60-70 atmospheres), significantly reducing energy costs. Third, yeast is a natural substance that is not harmful, whereas phosphoric acid used in hydration is corrosive and requires careful handling.

However, hydration has some advantages over fermentation. The hydration process is much faster than fermentation, which is a slow biological process. Additionally, hydration produces pure ethanol, while fermentation yields impure ethanol that requires further purification. Another consideration is that growing sugar cane for fermentation requires land that could otherwise be used for food production or livestock, whereas the hydration process doesn't have this limitation. Finally, hydration is a continuous process that can be operated constantly, while fermentation is typically a batch process that requires periodic setup and completion.

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: Explain why sodium chloride needs to be molten rather than solid for electrolysis to occur.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: In solid sodium chloride, ions are not free to move; in molten sodium chloride, ions are mobile and can conduct electricity.**

For electrolysis to occur, the ions must be free to move so they can migrate to the electrodes. In solid sodium chloride, the ions are held in fixed positions in a crystal lattice and cannot move. When sodium chloride is molten, the lattice breaks down and the ions become mobile, allowing them to carry electric current and participate in the electrolysis reaction.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the maximum volume, in dm3, of chlorine gas at rtp that can be obtained from 23.4 tonnes of molten sodium chloride. [1 tonne = 106 g] [Mr of NaCl = 58.5] [molar volume of chlorine at rtp = 24 dm3] Give your answer in standard form. volume = dm3
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 4.8 × 10⁶ dm³.**

*Step 1:* Calculate the amount of NaCl in moles:
Mass of NaCl = 23.4 tonnes = 23.4 × 10⁶ g
Moles of NaCl = (23.4 × 10⁶) ÷ 58.5 = 400,000 moles

*Step 2:* Determine the amount of Cl₂ produced:
From the equation 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂, 2 moles of NaCl produce 1 mole of Cl₂
Moles of Cl₂ = 400,000 ÷ 2 = 200,000 moles

*Step 3:* Calculate the volume of Cl₂ at rtp:
Volume = moles × molar volume = 200,000 × 24 = 4,800,000 dm³

*Step 4:* Give the answer in standard form:
4,800,000 dm³ = 4.8 × 10⁶ dm³

parts.problemMd: Calculate the amount, in moles, of NaOH in 30.40 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution. amount = mol
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.01596 mol.**

*Step 1 — moles = concentration × volume.* Table 2 gives the sodium hydroxide as 0.525 mol/dm³ and the mean titre as 30.40 cm³: 0.525 × 30.40 = 15.96, giving 15.96 ÷ 1000 = 0.01596 mol.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the amount, in moles, of H3PO4 in 25.0 cm3 of phosphoric acid. amount = mol
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.00532 mol.**

From the balanced equation 3NaOH + H₃PO₄ → Na₃PO₄ + 3H₂O, the mole ratio of NaOH to H₃PO₄ is 3:1. Therefore, the amount of H₃PO₄ is one-third the amount of NaOH.

amount of H₃PO₄ = amount of NaOH ÷ 3
amount of H₃PO₄ = 0.01596 mol ÷ 3 = 0.00532 mol

parts.problemMd: Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm3, of the phosphoric acid. concentration = mol/dm3
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.2128 mol/dm³.**

*Step 1 — moles of acid.* The equation 3NaOH + H₃PO₄ → Na₃PO₄ + 3H₂O shows three moles of NaOH reacting with every one mole of H₃PO₄, so from (d)(i): 0.01596 ÷ 3 = 0.00532 mol of phosphoric acid in the 25.0 cm³ sample.

*Step 2 — concentration.* 0.00532 × 1000 = 5.32 mol per 1000 cm³, and 5.32 ÷ 25.0 = 0.2128 mol/dm³.

The × 1000 scales the moles in 25.0 cm³ up to a whole dm³; dividing by 25.0 does the same job in a single step.

markPoints.textMd: 0.2128 (mol/dm3) OR answer to M1 evaluated correctly

parts.problemMd: The concentration of CH3COOH in vinegar can be found by titration with aqueous potassium hydroxide (KOH). The equation for the reaction is CH3COOH + KOH → CH3COOK + H2O In a titration, a 25.0 cm3 sample of vinegar is neutralised by 45.00 cm3 of KOH solution of concentration 0.400 mol/dm3. Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm3, of CH3COOH in this sample of vinegar. concentration = mol/dm3
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.72 mol/dm³.**

*Step 1 — moles of KOH:* moles = concentration × volume ÷ 1000, using the 45.00 cm³ of 0.400 mol/dm³ potassium hydroxide: 45.00 × 0.400 ÷ 1000 = 0.018 mol.

*Step 2 — moles of CH₃COOH:* the equation CH₃COOH + KOH → CH₃COOK + H₂O is a 1:1 ratio, so the 0.018 mol of KOH neutralised 0.018 mol of ethanoic acid.

*Step 3 — concentration of the acid:* the 25.0 cm³ sample is 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 dm³, and concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.018 ÷ 0.025 = 0.72 mol/dm³.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen gas and iodine gas react together to form hydrogen iodide gas. H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)

The pressure of an equilibrium mixture of the three gases is increased. Predict the effect of this change on the yield of hydrogen iodide at equilibrium, giving a reason for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: There is no effect on the yield of hydrogen iodide.**

According to Le Chatelier's principle, when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the system will adjust to minimize that change. In this case, the pressure is increased. However, the reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) has the same number of moles of gas on both sides of the equation (2 moles on the left and 2 moles on the right). Since there is no change in the number of moles of gas, increasing the pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium and therefore no effect on the yield of hydrogen iodide.

A catalyst works by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It increases the rate of both the forward and backward reactions by the same amount. parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen gas reacts with fluorine gas to form hydrogen fluoride gas. H2(g) + F2(g) → 2HF(g) The table gives some bond energies. Bond Bond energy in kJ/mol H H 436 F F 158 H F 562 Use the equation and the data in the table to calculate the enthalpy change (ΔH) in kJ/mol, for the reaction. Include a sign in your answer. ΔH = kJ/mol

![table — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.22)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2021-11/4CH1-2C/assets/asset_7_b_table.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = -530 kJ/mol.**

*Step 1:* Calculate the energy required to break the bonds in the reactants (bonds broken):
Bonds broken = H-H bond + F-F bond = 436 kJ/mol + 158 kJ/mol = 594 kJ/mol

*Step 2:* Calculate the energy released when forming the bonds in the products (bonds made):
Bonds made = 2 × H-F bond = 2 × 562 kJ/mol = 1124 kJ/mol

*Step 3:* Calculate the enthalpy change (ΔH) for the reaction:
ΔH = Energy absorbed (bonds broken) - Energy released (bonds made)
ΔH = 594 kJ/mol - 1124 kJ/mol = -530 kJ/mol

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes to give water and oxygen gas. The equation for this reaction is 2H2O2(aq) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g)

Three different solids are catalysts for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide solution. A student is given hydrogen peroxide solution and a sample of each of the solid catalysts. The student has a timer, a measuring cylinder, a balance and the apparatus shown in the diagram. Describe a method the student could use to find which of the three solids is the most effective catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide solution.

![apparatus — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.18) (same figure as asset_5_a_apparatus_stem)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2022-01/4CH1-2C/assets/asset_5_a_apparatus_stem.png)

![diagram — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.18) (same figure as asset_5_a_apparatus_stem)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2022-01/4CH1-2C/assets/asset_5_a_apparatus_stem.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** Measure the volume of oxygen gas produced in a given time for each catalyst using the same mass of catalyst and volume of hydrogen peroxide. The most effective catalyst will produce the most oxygen gas in the same time.

To find the most effective catalyst, the student should first add a measured volume of hydrogen peroxide solution to the conical flask. Then, add a measured mass of one of the solid catalysts to the flask and immediately start the timer. Measure the volume of oxygen gas collected in a fixed time interval, such as 1 minute. Record this volume. Repeat the experiment using the same mass of a different solid catalyst and the same volume of hydrogen peroxide. Continue this for all three catalysts. parts.problemMd: Write an ionic half‑equation for the formation of chlorine at the positive electrode.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−.**

At the positive electrode the chloride ions are oxidised: each Cl− ion loses its extra electron, and two chloride ions must be discharged to release one neutral chlorine molecule, Cl2. parts.problemMd: Show that the empirical formula of the compound is CH2O
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: CH₂O.**

*Step 1 — masses from the percentages:* treat the printed percentages as masses in grams, so a sample of the compound contains 40 g of C, 6.7 g of H and 53.3 g of O.

*Step 2 — moles:* divide each mass by its relative atomic mass — never by the atomic numbers. Moles of C = 40 ÷ 12 = 3.33; moles of H = 6.7 ÷ 1 = 6.7; moles of O = 53.3 ÷ 16 = 3.33.

*Step 3 — simplest ratio:* the mole ratio is 3.33 : 6.7 : 3.33; dividing every term by the smallest gives 3.33 ÷ 3.33 = 1 and 6.7 ÷ 3.33 ≈ 2, so the whole-number ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.

That division delivers the ratio of atoms in the compound, and the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 is the empirical formula CH₂O.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: shake ethene with bromine water and the bromine water decolourises — it turns colourless.**

parts.problemMd:
This question is about metals.

Explain why metals are malleable.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: metals are malleable because their layers of positive ions can slide over one another.**
In a metal the atoms (positive ions) sit in neat, regular layers, held together by a sea of delocalised electrons. When a force is applied, whole layers of ions can slide over one another and settle into new positions without shattering the structure, so the metal bends and flattens into a new shape instead of breaking like a brittle solid.

parts.problemMd: Explain why molten sodium chloride conducts electricity.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: because its ions are free to move.**
Melting has broken down the regular lattice of sodium chloride, so the sodium ions and chloride ions are no longer locked in fixed positions. These mobile, charged particles — the ions, not electrons — can move through the liquid and carry charge from one electrode to the other, which is exactly what an electric current needs, so the molten salt conducts.

parts.problemMd: Explain how sodium metal forms at the negative electrode.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the positive sodium ions (Na+) are attracted to the negative electrode, where they each gain an electron and become sodium atoms.**
The Na+ cations move through the molten salt towards the negative electrode because opposite charges attract. On arrival, each Na+ ion gains one electron — it is reduced: Na+ + e− → Na. Neutral sodium atoms build up there, and molten sodium metal collects beneath the electrode.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−**
At the positive electrode each chloride ion is oxidised: it loses its extra electron. parts.problemMd: Give a reason why sodium metal does not form in the electrolysis of an aqueous solution of sodium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is produced at the negative electrode instead.**
In aqueous solution there are hydrogen ions (from the water) as well as sodium ions. At the negative electrode it is the less reactive positive ions that are discharged: sodium sits higher than hydrogen in the reactivity series, so the sodium ions stay in solution while the hydrogen ions are discharged, giving off bubbles of hydrogen gas rather than sodium metal.

parts.problemMd: Name ester A.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethyl ethanoate.**
Ester names have two words: first the alkyl group supplied by the alcohol, then the carboxylate supplied by the acid. The ethanol contributes the two-carbon ethyl group and the ethanoic acid contributes the ethanoate part, so ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + water.

parts.problemMd: The reaction mixture is kept in a sealed container until dynamic equilibrium is reached. State what is meant by the term dynamic equilibrium.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: dynamic equilibrium means the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.**
In the sealed container the ester forms in the forward reaction and breaks back apart in the reverse reaction. At equilibrium the two rates are equal — the system is dynamic because both reactions are still happening — and each substance is made exactly as fast as it is used up, so the concentrations of ethanoic acid, ethanol, ester A and water stay constant (constant, though not necessarily equal).
