parts.problemMd: A student is given an aqueous solution of chlorine and an aqueous solution of sodium iodide. The student mixes the two solutions. Explain the colour change that occurs.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the mixture turns from colourless to brown, because iodine is displaced.**

Chlorine is the more reactive halogen, so it takes iodine's place: the chlorine reacts with the iodide ions, iodine (I₂) is displaced and shows itself as the brown colour. Displacement only works in one direction — the more reactive halogen always wins — so if you added iodine solution to sodium chloride instead, nothing would happen, because iodine is less reactive than chlorine.

parts.problemMd: Explain why an alloy is less malleable than a pure metal.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: in an alloy the different-sized atoms distort the regular layers, so the layers can no longer slide over one another easily — the alloy is less malleable.**

In a pure metal every atom is the same size and the atoms sit in neat, regular rows. When a force is applied, whole layers of atoms can slide past one another, so the metal bends without shattering — that is malleability. In steel the carbon atoms are much smaller than the iron atoms, so they wedge into the gaps and the regular arrangement of the atoms becomes irregular and distorted. That misfit makes it more difficult for the layers to slide, so the alloy holds its shape instead of denting.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the insoluble salt, lead(II) bromide. Lead(II) bromide can be made by a precipitation reaction. This is the equation for the reaction. Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → PbBr2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)

Describe how solutions of lead nitrate and potassium bromide can be used to make a pure, dry sample of lead(II) bromide.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: mix the two solutions, filter off the precipitate, wash it, then dry it.**

*Step 1 — mix:* add the lead nitrate solution to the potassium bromide solution and stir; they react and insoluble lead(II) bromide forms as a precipitate: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → PbBr₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq).

*Step 2 — filter:* pour the mixture through filter paper. The solid lead bromide is caught on the paper and the soluble potassium nitrate stays in the solution that runs through.

*Step 3 — wash:* rinse the solid on the paper with a little deionised water to wash away any potassium nitrate solution clinging to the crystals.

*Step 4 — dry:* leave the washed solid to dry in a warm place (a low oven works, or dab it dry with filter paper). That leaves a pure, dry sample of lead(II) bromide.

Do not try to evaporate the mixture instead — evaporating to dryness would trap soluble potassium nitrate among the crystals, so the sample would not be pure.

parts.problemMd: A solution containing 0.150 mol of lead(II) nitrate is reacted with an excess of potassium bromide solution. A mass of 49.6 g of pure, dry lead(II) bromide is produced. Show, by calculation, that the percentage yield of lead(II) bromide is 90.1%. [for PbBr2 , Mr = 367]
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 90.1%.**

*Step 1 — maximum moles of lead(II) bromide:* the equation Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → PbBr₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq) links lead(II) nitrate to lead(II) bromide in a 1 : 1 ratio, so 0.150 mol of lead nitrate could make at most 0.150 mol of PbBr₂.

*Step 2 — theoretical mass:* mass = moles × Mr: 0.150 × 367 = 55.05 g.

*Step 3 — percentage yield:* actual mass ÷ theoretical mass, expressed as a percentage:

49.6 ÷ 55.05 × 100 = 90.1%

The student harvested 49.6 g of lead(II) bromide, which is 90.1% of the 55.05 g the equation predicts — the rest was lost on the filter paper and in the filtrate.

parts.problemMd: Explain why lithium is less reactive than potassium. Refer to atomic structure in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: lithium is less reactive because its outer electron is more strongly attracted to the nucleus, so it is less easily lost.**

Lithium has fewer occupied shells than potassium — its outer electron sits in the second shell, while potassium's sits in the fourth. Being closer to the nucleus, and shielded from it by fewer inner shells of electrons, the lithium outer electron feels a stronger attraction to the positive nucleus. A more strongly held electron needs more energy to be pulled away, so lithium's outer electron is less easily lost to water than potassium's — and losing that outer electron is what the reaction with water depends on, which is why potassium reacts much more violently.

parts.problemMd: Show that the molar enthalpy change, ΔH, for the reaction is −119 kJ / mol.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −119 kJ/mol, and the bond energies show exactly where that number comes from.**

*Step 1 — bonds broken in the reactants:* 2 mol of H–H bonds plus 1 mol of C≡O bond: 436 + 436 + 1072 = 1944 kJ/mol absorbed.

*Step 2 — bonds made in the product:* methanol, CH₃OH, contains 3 C–H bonds, 1 C–O bond and 1 O–H bond: 414 + 414 + 414 + 358 + 463 = 2063 kJ/mol released.

*Step 3 — the difference:* 2063 − 1944 = 119 kJ/mol more energy is released making bonds than is absorbed breaking them, so the overall change is ΔH = −119 kJ/mol.

parts.problemMd: Explain why this reaction is exothermic.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: because more energy is given out when the new bonds are made than is taken in when the original bonds are broken.**

Breaking bonds always takes in energy (it is endothermic): here the 2 H–H bonds and the C≡O bond absorb 1944 kJ/mol. Making bonds always releases energy (it is exothermic): the 3 C–H, 1 C–O and 1 O–H bonds of methanol release 2063 kJ/mol. Since 2063 is the larger figure, the energy released making bonds beats the energy absorbed breaking them, so there is a net transfer of energy to the surroundings — the reaction is exothermic and ΔH comes out negative.

- use a measuring cylinder to transfer 25 cm3 of potassium hydroxide solution to a conical flask
- add two drops of an indicator
- fill a burette with phosphoric acid solution and record the initial reading on the burette
- add the acid to the conical flask

**Answer: two improvements, each given as a pair of points — the change you make and the reason it gives more accurate results.**

parts.problemMd: Use the bond energies to show that the molar enthalpy change, ΔH , is about −1300 kJ / mol.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −1263 kJ/mol, i.e. about −1300 kJ/mol.**
*Step 1 — bonds broken (energy taken in):* C₂H₅OH holds 5 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C–O and 1 O–H, and the 3O₂ adds 3 O=O, so from the table 346 + 5 × 414 + 358 + 463 + 3 × 498 = 4731 kJ/mol.
*Step 2 — bonds made (energy given out):* the products hold 4 C=O bonds in the 2CO₂ and 6 O–H bonds in the 3H₂O: 4 × 804 + 6 × 463 = 5994 kJ/mol.
*Step 3 — the enthalpy change:* 5994 − 4731 = 1263 kJ/mol more energy is given out than taken in.
ΔH is therefore negative: ΔH = −1263 kJ/mol — about −1300 kJ/mol, exactly the value the question asks you to show.

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of bonds broken and bonds made, why this reaction is exothermic.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: more energy is given out when the new bonds are made than is taken in when the original bonds are broken.**
Breaking bonds is endothermic — it takes in energy: 4731 kJ/mol to break the C–H, C–C, C–O, O–H and O=O bonds in the reactants. Making bonds is exothermic — it releases energy: 5994 kJ/mol as the new C=O and O–H bonds form in the CO₂ and H₂O. parts.problemMd:
This question is about aluminium.

Why does solid aluminium conduct electricity?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — electrons are free to move in the solid.**

Solid aluminium is a metal: its outer electrons are delocalised, meaning they are not attached to any one aluminium atom, so they drift through the whole lattice and carry charge from place to place. That moving charge is the electric current.

Why the other options fail: B adds neutrons to the claim, but neutrons sit inside the nucleus and are never free to move, so they cannot carry charge. C adds protons, but protons are also locked inside the nucleus and cannot flow through the solid. D claims the ions move, but in solid aluminium the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice — only the electrons flow (ions only become mobile in a molten metal or in solution).

markPoints.textMd: Answer A: electrons are free to move in the solid

parts.problemMd: Explain why aluminium is malleable.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: aluminium is malleable because its layers of atoms can slide over one another.** In the metallic lattice the aluminium atoms (positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons) are arranged in neat layers. When a force is applied, those layers can slide over one another and settle into new positions without the metallic bonding breaking, so the metal bends and reshapes instead of shattering. It is the layers that slide — not the electrons, and not any negative ions, since there are none in a metal lattice.

parts.problemMd: Why is aluminium not extracted by heating aluminium oxide with carbon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — aluminium is more reactive than carbon.**

Carbon removes oxygen from the oxides of metals that are less reactive than itself. Aluminium sits above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot pull the oxygen away from aluminium oxide — heating the two together simply gives no reaction, and electrolysis is needed instead.

Why the other options fail: B says carbon is an oxidising agent, but in these reactions carbon gains oxygen, so it is acting as the reducing agent, not an oxidising agent. C says the reaction has a low activation energy, but the opposite is true — the barrier is a very high activation energy, which ordinary heating cannot supply. D says the reaction is explosive, but nothing that dramatic happens: carbon and aluminium oxide simply do not react with each other.

parts.problemMd: In a different experiment, the student burns 0.75 g of propanol. The heat energy change for this experiment is 19 500 J. Calculate the molar enthalpy change, ΔH, in kJ / mol. Include a sign in your answer. [for propanol, Mr = 60] ΔH = kJ / mol

**Answer: ΔH = −1560 kJ/mol.**

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of bonds broken and bonds made, why this reaction is exothermic.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: combustion is exothermic because more energy is given out when the new bonds are made than is taken in when the original bonds are broken.** Breaking bonds always takes in energy, and making bonds always releases energy. Here the bonds made in the products — the C=O bonds in the carbon dioxide and the O−H bonds in the water — release more energy than was needed to break the bonds in the ethanol and the oxygen. There is a net release of energy to the surroundings, so the mixture warms up: that surplus is what makes the reaction exothermic.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about sugars.

Sugar A has this percentage composition by mass. C = 44.7% H = 7.5% O = 47.8% Determine the empirical formula of sugar A. [Ar values: C = 12 H=1 O = 16] empirical formula =
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the empirical formula of sugar A is C₅H₁₀O₄.**

*Step 1 — amount of each element:* divide each percentage by its Ar value (never the other way up in the calculation, and never by the atomic number):
C: 44.7 ÷ 12 = 3.725
H: 7.5 ÷ 1 = 7.5
O: 47.8 ÷ 16 = 2.99

*Step 2 — divide by the smallest:* 3.725 ÷ 2.99 ≈ 1.25 and 7.5 ÷ 2.99 ≈ 2.5, so the ratio of C : H : O is 1.25 : 2.5 : 1.

*Step 3 — clear the decimals:* multiply every part by 4 — 1.25 × 4 = 5 and 2.5 × 4 = 10 and 1 × 4 = 4 — so the whole-number ratio is 5 : 10 : 4.

The correct empirical formula is therefore C₅H₁₀O₄.

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by the term dynamic equilibrium.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: dynamic equilibrium means the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.** Both reactions never stop — molecules keep forming products in one direction and breaking back down in the other, at an equal rate — so in the closed system there is no overall change in the amounts of reactants and products. Constant does not mean equal: the two concentrations stay steady, but they do not have to be the same as each other.

parts.problemMd: Explain the effects on rate of reaction and yield of products if the temperature is changed to 1000 °C but the pressure is kept at 10 atm. rate of reaction yield of products
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the rate of reaction increases, but the yield of products decreases.**

Rate of reaction: raising the temperature from 800 °C to 1000 °C gives every particle more kinetic energy, so many more collisions have energy greater than the activation energy, and the faster-moving particles also collide more often. More frequent successful collisions per unit time means the rate of reaction increases.

Yield of products: the forward reaction 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O is exothermic — ΔH is −900 kJ/mol, and a negative ΔH means energy is released going forwards. When the temperature is raised, the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction, which is the backwards reaction here, to absorb the extra energy. So the position of equilibrium moves to the left and the yield of products decreases, even though equilibrium is reached sooner. The pressure stays at 10 atm throughout, so pressure causes no extra change in the yield.

parts.problemMd: Lowering the pressure would increase the yield of products. Give a reason why a lower pressure is not used.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: because the rate of reaction would be too slow.** At a lower pressure the gas particles are spread further apart, so collisions between the molecules happen less often and less frequently per second. The plant would then make nitrogen monoxide — and downstream, nitric acid — far too slowly to be economic, even though a lower pressure would raise the yield.

parts.problemMd: A student does a titration using dilute nitric acid and a solution of sodium hydroxide with a known concentration. These are the first four steps in the student’s method. • add 25.0 cm3 of nitric acid to a conical flask • add sodium hydroxide solution to a burette and record the initial volume • add a few drops of methyl orange indicator to the flask • use the burette to add sodium hydroxide solution to the flask until the indicator changes colour Describe how the student could modify their method to obtain an accurate value for the volume of sodium hydroxide solution needed to neutralise 25.0 cm3 of nitric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: rinse the burette with the sodium hydroxide solution before filling, measure the acid with a volumetric pipette, rinse the conical flask with distilled water, add the sodium hydroxide dropwise near the end point while swirling, and repeat the titration until the results are concordant.**

Rinsing the burette with sodium hydroxide before filling removes any water or air bubbles left inside, so the solution that runs out is at its true concentration. Measuring the 25.0 cm3 of nitric acid with a volumetric pipette fixes that volume much more precisely than pouring. Rinsing the conical flask with distilled or deionised water clears out residues without touching the amount of acid, because the water adds no extra acid to neutralise. A white tile under the flask makes the methyl orange colour change easy to see against a pale background. Swirling the flask as the alkali runs in keeps every drop mixed through the solution, and near the end point the sodium hydroxide should be added dropwise so the first permanent colour change is caught exactly. Finally, record the burette reading at that end point and repeat the whole titration until two results agree within 0.1–0.2 cm3 — those concordant titres give an accurate value for the volume of sodium hydroxide that neutralises the acid.
